# Maṅgala Sutta (Kp 5 (PTS Kp 2))

**ID:** Kp 5 (PTS Kp 2)
**Section:** Khuddakapāṭha (kp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Maṅgala Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** True Blessings
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/kp5
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0501m.mul4.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Maṅgala Sutta* (Kp 5) is a renowned discourse comprising a brief introductory setting and twelve verses (often enumerated in commentarial traditions as eleven stanzas of blessings) in which the Buddha delineates the highest auspicious blessings (*maṅgala*) [Buswell & Lopez 2014; von Hinüber 1996; Powers 2016]. In response to a deity's question, the Buddha presents a progressive exposition of thirty-eight skillful practices and virtues, beginning with fundamental mundane and social obligations—such as avoiding fools, associating with the wise, honoring parents, and practicing generosity—and culminating in unshakeable mental tranquility, purification, and the attainment of *nibbāna* [Buswell & Lopez 2014; Walker; SuttaCentral]. Within the Pali canon, the discourse occurs twice in identical form: here as the fifth text of the *Khuddakapāṭha* and as the fourth sutta of the Cūḷavagga in the *Sutta-nipāta* (Snp 2.4) [Anālayo 2018; Walker; SuttaCentral].

Widely recognized as one of the most influential and frequently recited texts across Theravāda Southeast Asia and Sri Lanka, the *Maṅgala Sutta* forms an essential part of the *paritta* (protective chanting) collection [Powers 2016; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. In Burma, it historically served as a foundational reader in childhood monastic and lay curricula [Turner 2009]. The text generated substantial exegetical literature, notably the massive sixteenth-century Northern Thai commentary *Maṅgalatthadīpanī* by Sirimaṅgala of Chiang Mai, which continues to form a central component of Thai monastic education [von Hinüber 1996; Buswell & Lopez 2014; Heim 2004; Boriharnwanaket].

Curated parallels include its canonical duplicate Snp 2.4 and a passage-level Chinese parallel in the *Dharmapada Avadāna Sūtra* (T 211.39) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus confirms the comprehensive match with Snp 2.4 (§0.1–14.1, similarity 0.98), notes formulaic reuse of the introductory framing with the *Devatā Saṁyutta* (SN 1) and *Devaputta Saṁyutta* (SN 2), and identifies cross-language alignments with Tibetan canonical texts, chief among them the Kangyur's *Mahāmaṅgala-sūtra* (D 43) [DharmaNexus], which was translated from Pali by the Sinhalese master Ānandaśrī [Gaffney 2003].
